The Wavlink WL-UTD58-M is our go-to pick for a value-packed Thunderbolt 5 dock among our roundup of the best Thunderbolt 5 docks overall. It's on sale for its previous all-time low price of $179.40 on a lighting sale, which, at the time of writing, is 39% claimed.

The Wavlink WL-UTD58-M is a Thunderbolt 5 dock with three downstream TB5 ports, four USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A ports, 2.5G LAN, SD/MicroSD 4.0, 3.5mm, and an include M.2 2280 slot that supports up to PCIe 4.0 x4 8TB drives.

As a Thunderbolt 5 dock, you get up to 8K at 144Hz with a single display (up to three at 4K144) and 140W of power delivery. The single upstream TB5 port operates at 120Gbps, while the three downstream ports operate at up to 80Gbps. The dock also includes a 2.5Gb RJ45 connection, four USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A ports, 3.5mm mic/audio combo jack, and both a SD and MicroSD 4.0 slot.

On the bottom of the dock, there's space for a M.2 2280 NVMe SSD that operates at up to 64Gbps (PCIe 4.0 x4), with up to 8TB drives supported. — Jake Roach

It's hard to criticize Corsair for taking design inspiration from the Fractal North with its Frame 4000D Wood RS — the entire PC case market did — and you shouldn't let the trimmings distract from the quality case that is the Frame 4000D at its core. It's a great chassis, and it's on sale for a great price at just $99.99 at Newegg, 23% off its MSRP and $16 less than what you'll spend on the Fractal North on sale elsewhere.

The Corsair Frame 4000D Wood RS is a midtower PC case that support ITX up to E-ATX motherboards, and it comes with four RS-120 PWM 120mm fans pre-installed.

We found that the case is an excellent thermal performer in our Corsair Frame 4000D case review, and it's extremely flexible with modular components and Corsair's InfiniRail mounting systems for fans. The side panels are flexible, too. You can swap out the wood front if you choose, or pick up a tempered glass side panel that has a cutout for mounting the Xeneon Edge touch display.

This sale includes the Frame 4000D Wood RS with four pre-installed RS120 PWM fans. As usual, it comes with the marquee features of the Frame 4000D, including the built-in, adjustable GPU support bracket. — Jake Roach

The Cooler Master Hyper 212 throughout its various iterations is a legendary CPU cooler for a reason. It's simple and effective, and best of all, it's dirt cheap. The upgraded Hyper 212 3DHP, complete with an aRGB fan, is on a clearance sale at Woot for just $24.99, which is going for the next three days (unlikely) or until the cooler sells out (more likely).

The Hyper 212 3DHP aRGB is a CPU cooler for LGA 1851, 1700, 1200, 115x, AM5, and AM4 sockets. It includes two CM 3DHP heatpipes and an aRGB fan.

The innovation with this cooler is in the name: it's Cooler Master's 3DHP heatpipes. Instead of a U shape like a traditional heatpipe, CM's are shaped like a trident. And, as you can read about in our Cooler Master Hyper 212 3DHP review, this design allows Cooler Master to achieve superior thermal performance with two 3DHP pipes compared to four standard pipes.

Our resident cooling expert Albert Thomas said the 3DHP pipes "might be the most significant air cooler release in the past decade" against the backdrop of seemingly endless Hyper 212 variations. The cooler works with LGA 1851, 1700, 1200, 151x, AM5, and AM4 platforms. — Jake Roach

Intel's latest Wildcat Lake chips for budget laptops do things a bit differently. Instead of leveraging older technology, Wildcat Lake is built on Intel's latest 18A node, the same process found in Panther Lake, just with a number of corners cut under the food. Most Wildcat Lake laptops run around $600 to $700 normally in their base configurations, or about $550 on sale. But Acer has the Swift Air 14 marked down to just $419.99 at Best Buy if you act fast; the deal is only going through the end of the day.

This Acer Swift Air 14 comes with an Intel Core 5 320 chip, 8GB of LPDDR5 memory, and 512GB of storage.

As you can see in our Acer Swift Air 14 review from just a few months ago, we were happy to recommend the laptop at full price. Unsurprisingly, the Core 5 320 chip at the heart of the machine won't turn heads with its performance, but it's enough to power through basic browser-based and local productivity workloads. The laptop mainly stood out on its premium trimmings between its long battery life, aluminum chassis, and Thunderbolt 4 support.

In a like-for-like scenario where all of these Core 5 320 designs with 8GB of memory clock in around $700, we push most folks toward the Dell XPS 13 (linked above for $550). On this deep of a discount, however, there's no question that the Swift Air 14 wins the day. — Jake Roach

A unique novelty gift, or a quirky upgrade to any setup, this tiny keyboard has just two bottons: Copy and Paste. This means you have a dedicated keyboard for two of the most used functions on any keyboard.

This two-key keyboard includes mechanical switches bound to copy and paste by default. However, you can rebind the keys to whatever you like.

Naturally, this is really just a tiny enclosure and two key switches. The beauty of it is that you don't actually have to use it for copy and paste, even though the buttons are labelled as such. You can reassign the keys to whatever you want, even to macros. Just $11 makes this a perfect stocking filler or impulse buy. - Stephen Warwick

In the run-up to Black Friday, we rounded up the cheapest prices we could find on PCIe 4.0 SSDs, all under $0.15 per GB, and unfortunately, a lot of those deals have sold out. The Team Group T-Force G50 4TB is still going strong, however, and it's easily the best deal on an SSD we've seen during the entire Black Friday/Cyber Monday shopping event at just $0.10 per GB.

This T-Force G50 Evo offers sequential read speeds of 5,000 MB/s and write speeds of up to 4,800 MB/s.

Earlier in the week, the Kingston NV3 1TB was $140, now it's $160. The Biwin Black Opal NV7400 was marked down in both its 1TB and 2TB capacities, and now you'll only find the 512GB version (no less for more than the 1TB deal). That makes the fact that this T-Force G50 deal is still going all the more impressive.

It's a midrange PCIe 4.0 drive offering sequential reads of up to 5,000 MB/s and sequential writes up to 4,700 MB/s. Capacity for the price is the draw here, however. At 4TB and $399.99, the G50 is cheaper than even some SATA drives right now. — Jake Roach

A great deal that we covered earleir this week is still in stock and on sale as Amazon pivots to Cyber Monday. This UGREEN Nexode is a 20,000 mAh battery bank that serves as a portable travel charger for all your devices. It comes with up to 130W of combined power, and two USB-C cables, as well as a USB-A port.

The UGREEN Nexode 20000 mAh power bank supports up to 130W of combined power output and features two USB-C and one USB-A port.

You get a power output of 100W from the first USB-C port, and a further 30W from the second. UGREEN touts that this device can fully charge a MacBook up to 1.3 times, or an iPhone 16 Pro up to 3.7 times. There's an LED display to give you information on charge level, output, and time remaining before you run out of juice. - Stephen Warwick

You can never have too many good chargers by your side. Anker's 4-port GaN 140W charger can handle charging at up to 140W across two USB-C ports, while a third USB-C can handle phone charging at up to 40W, and for any other devices, USB-A charging at 33W. Now under $60 at Amazon and sporting two different colorways, you can add another charger to your arsenal for less.

The Anker 140W charging brick offers a total of four ports across two USB-C ports capable of up to 140W charging, one USB-C port at 40W, and a USB-A port at 33W. The device has a display, which reads out per-port wattages on the fly.

Ensuring that you get the fastest charging speeds doesn't have to be difficult, as the device also ships with a handy little display where you can see the charging status of each port, in addition to a wattage readout. 140W is indeed more than enough to charge an ultraportable laptop on the fly, including devices like a MacBook Air or Pro.

To get the fastest speeds out of the unit, make sure that you're not overpopulating the two fully-featured USB-C ports; if you use both of them at the same time, then you split the total max wattage across them at a maximum of 70W each. Otherwise, this is a solid deal on a charging brick that, quite frankly, everyone needs. The device also comes with an 18-month warranty from Anker for that little bit of extra peace of mind. — Sayem Ahmed

Meta's more affordable VR headset is back down to its sub-$300 price at Newegg. For that, you get the same CPU, RAM, and storage as the more expensive Meta Quest 3, as well as better battery life. The difference is that the Quest 3S has a much more modest display with a slightly narrower FOV.

The Meta Quest 3S is the most affordable VR headset from Meta. Despite that, it still comes with the same CPU, RAM, and base storage as the most expensive Meta Quest 3, while also offering a slightly better battery life.

This Newegg deal gets you a 128GB Quest 3S, including GOLF+ and 1,800 game credits to get you started. It offers 1,832 x 1,920 pixels per eye resolution, equivalent of 773 PPI. By comparison, the more expensive Quest 3 is 2,064 x 2,208 pixels per eye or 1218 PPI, 30% more. Battery life is good for about two and a half hours, although your mileage will of course vary depending on use case. - Stephen Warwick

Woot has a massive saving on this Keychron Q2Wired Custom Mechanical Keyboard. Usually priced at $199.99, this new keyboard is now just $74.99, a 63% discount. You get a 65% layout keyboard with a solid aluminum frame. My own personal keyboard is a Keychron and I love how solid it and easy to type on it is.

Get a 65% layout mechanical keyboard with QMK and VIA support for programming and remapping. Pre-installed with Gateron G Pro mechanical linear red switches, can be hot-swapped.

The keys on this keyboard are Gateron G Pro mechanical linear red switches with up to 50 million keystroke lifespan. QMK and VIA support means you can program and remap every key on this keyboard to your liking on macOS, Windows, or Linux. The double-gasket design is complemented by sound-absorbing case foam, and the caps are double-shot PBT to ensure they don't wear down. Use code PCGAMING at checkout for an extra 20% off. - Stephen Warwick

Building a DIY PC is extremely difficult these days, but we've managed to cobble together a 4K gaming PC for less than $2,500. Naturally, it includes 32GB of DDR5 RAM that costs over $400 and a 2TB SSD, but we have saved some money elsewhere.

Our savings come largely from the Intel Core Ultra 7 270K, which Intel is giving away for pennies on the dollar this weekend. With 24 cores and 24 threads, this PC combines with the Radeon RX 9070 XT's 16GB of VRAM for strong 4K gaming performance.

Intel's Core Ultra 7 270K Plus CPU delivers Core Ultra 9 performance for Core Ultra 5 money right now. 24 cores and peak boost speeds of up to 5.5 GHz deliver incredible single- and multi-threaded performance.

Arctic's Liquid Freezer Pro 360mm liquid cooler is one of our favorites for both cooling performance and value, and it's as affordable as ever right now.

Asus' ROG Strix Z890-E Gaming Wifi board offers incredible peripheral and storage expansion options at an incredibly low price after promo code BFEF196 at Newegg.

Klevv's Fit V DDR5-6000 RAM kit is as good as any amid the AI supply crunch. Check out our list of the best RAM deals for an up-to-the-minute look at the best prices on similar kits.

We consider 2TB of capacity non-negotiable for a high-end gaming PC build like this, so we chose Silicon Power's P34A60 for its strong value rather than its absolute performance.

XFX's spiffy triple-fan RX 9070 XT will deliver strong gaming performance at 1440p and even 4K, and FSR 4.1 upscaling can give you an extra performance boost if native rendering proves too heavy a load.

Corsair's handsome Frame 4000D RS ARGB case gives us plenty of room for the high-end components in this build, and its trio of ARGB fans is a nice bonus.

MSI's MPG A1000GS PSU offers 80 Plus Gold efficiency, fully modular cabling, two 12V-2x6 connectors, and enough eight-pin PCIe connectors to power modern graphics cards from both AMD and Nvidia. You can redeem a $10 rebate card for a lower price.

Buying one giant ultrawide monitor is a great way to save space and upgrade your productivity. This monster is a 49-inch Odyssey OLED G9 from Samsung. The QD OLED panel refreshes at 144Hz, with a 0.03ms response time.

The Samsung Odyssey OLED G9 is a 49-inch monitor with a 32:9 aspect ratio. It comes with a resolution of 5120 x 1440 and a refresh rate of 144Hz.

The curve on this monitor is a more subtle 1800R curve, rather than 1000R. With its 5120 x 1440p resolution, this monitor is the equivalent of putting two 27-inch gaming monitors side-by-side. The convenience of a large ultrawide display means it takes up much less space on your desk, with only one stand to speak of. It also requires just the one power outlet.

If you're happy to spend a bit more, the G93SC version comes with a 240Hz refresh rate for $854.98. - Stephen Warwick

We love a Hoto screwdriver at Tom's Hardware, and this PixelDrive is the company's latest and greatest. This all-singing, all-dancing screwdriver comes with a smart display, 30 bits, six torque settings, and an LED light. It's a great impulse purchase for PC and hardware DIYers, or a great gift for someone who loves tinkering.

Get a Hoto screwdriver with smart display, 30 bits, LED light, and six torque settings.

With adjustable torque settings this screwdriver is equally useful for delicate electronics work as it is for DIY and home repairs. Beyond the torque settings, there's also a two-speed Smart Trigger, where half a press gets you an 80RPM low speed turn, while a full press gets you the 200 RPM high speed mode. You get 30 bits, 20 long bits and 10 short bits, a total of 20 different types, housed in a unique triple-layer cylinder, so there's no bulky box to take up space in your tool shed.

The battery is a 2,000 mAh and there's also 360 degree LED lighting so you can see clearly whatever you're working on. - Stephen Warwick

Alrighty, we might have just shown you a drive that's $20 more expensive, with slower speeds, but our team of intrepid deal-hunters have just discovered a fantastic offer on modern, PCIe Gen 5 storage. MSI's Spatium M560 2TB PCIe 5.0 drive offers rapid speeds of up to 10,300 MB/s read and up to 8,700 MB/s write. This DRAM-less drive operates on the Phison PS5031-E31T controller. It's not the highest-caliber PCIe 5.0 drive out there, but at a price like this, it's difficult to refute.

MSI's Spatium M560 PCIe Gen 5 SSD makes use of the PCIe Gen 5 x4 interface, alongside a Phison PS5031-E31T controller. Offering 10,300 MB/s read and up to 8,700 MB/s write speeds, the DRAM-less drive is rated for an industry-standard 1,200 TBW of endurance and sips on power, running at 5.9W maximum. It also comes with a five-year limited warranty.

The single-sided SSD here is pretty easy to cool on integrated motherboard heatsinks, and it delivers much more throughput when compared to older-gen PCIe Gen 4 drives, and given the pricing tier that this drive has reached thanks to MSI's Black Friday weekend deals, you can save hundreds of dollars on storage. There's no included heatsink in the box, and a DRAM-less SSD does come with its own downsides when writing larger files (think several hundred GB and more), but if that scenario is unlikely on your end, then this drive is well suited for populating your main motherboard slot. — Sayem Ahmed

Unlike our last spotlight, which offered slower storage, getting a modern NVMe drive will boast unholy speeds, especially if you're looking at a PCIe 5.0 drive. However, for this one, we're looking at a couple of Silicon Power's 2TB SSDs: first, a 2TB PCIe Gen 3 drive, which is priced at $209.99 over at Newegg, netting you an effective price of 11 cents per gigabyte of rapid storage.

The Silicon Power SU002TBP34A60M28SN offers 2TB of NVMe storage at PCIe Gen 3 speeds, with read speeds of up to 2200 MB/s and write speeds of 1,600 MB/s. It's not the fastest drive out there, but it makes up for it with capacity. The drive offers up to 1,200 TBW of rated endurance and is a DRAM-less drive sporting 3D TLC NAND.

As for the other drive Silicon Power is offering, it's the company's UD90 PCIe 4.0 drive, which will offer much faster speeds than the drive we listed previously. Of course, that comes at a premium. You'll pay $289.79 for the privilege of getting up to 5,000 MB/s on reads and 4,800 MB/s on writes, which is a significant jump, if you're willing to part with an extra 90 bucks.

The DRAM-less drive offers up to 5,000 MB/s on reads and 4,800 MB/s on writes, with a 2 TB capacity. With 1,200 TBW rated endurance and a five-year limited warranty, this is a solid option for someone looking to beef up their PC's storage.

The single-sided Silicon Power PCIe Gen 4 drive here offers decent speeds, a good five-year limited warranty, and above all else, a good amount of capacity. As NAND prices have continued to soar over the past year and change, getting a deal one an NVMe SSD doesn't have to bankrupt you. There's no included heatsink on each of these drives either, so you'll either have to pick one up for yourself, or check out if you've got a built in NVMe heatsink on your PC's motherboard. — Sayem Ahmed

Grabbing yourself some storage this Black Friday weekend doesn't have to be a struggle with 27% off a 6TB WD My Passport external HDD. The drive itself comes in at a 2.5-inch form factor, so you won't need any external power source to hook things up. When factoring in the discounted price of $239.99, it works out to just three cents per gigabyte, which is a solid deal in 2026, when we've seen skyrocketing HDD prices.

The 2.5-inch drive within the WD My Passport offers 6TB of storage, in addition to a USB 3.0 Micro-B port on the drive, which can be hooked up to your devices via a USB-A port.

We reviewed this drive back in 2024, and we awarded it four out of five stars. You can view some of our benchmarks above, where you can see what real-world performance looks like. Don't expect miracles from a spinning disk running over a USB 3.0 connector here, but with the storage volume available here, you could do much worse than this.

This drive is ideal for large media libraries that you need to take on the go, or for storing large projects like video files, which you need to access on the fly. Just make sure you go in with the expectation that the drive offers meagre speeds. But what it lacks in speed, it makes up for in pure volume. — Sayem Ahmed

Apple's MacBook Air is pretty much my default answer whenever someone asks me what laptop they should buy. Sporting an all-aluminum chassis, a solid piece of Apple Silicon beneath it, a Retina display, and a 12MP camera, Apple's mid-tier system is an attractive buy for almost every user. The 13-inch model is currently down to just $999 across all color variants, and if you want the 15-inch model of the M5 Air, then you'll pay only $1,199, taking $300 off both models.

The 15-inch model on sale is now cheaper than what the 13-inch model usually retails for, making the system a bit of a bargain, especially if you have friends or relatives already locked into the Apple ecosystem looking for a simple laptop to upgrade to; it's impossible to miss by recommending them an Apple MacBook Air. Also, no other trackpad feels quite as nice as what Apple offers, and the speakers on the chassis are very good, considering how tightly packed the system is.

The M5 MacBook Air offers 512GB of storage, a 13-inch Retina display, and a 10-core CPU and 8-Core GPU with 16GB of unified memory that can take on pretty much all everyday tasks with ease.

The M5 MacBook Air sports 512GB of storage, a 15.3-inch Retina display, 16GB of unified memory for multitasking, a 10-core CPU and 8-Core GPU, with extra space dedicated to Neural Accelerators for use with Apple Intelligence.

If you're wondering what we thought about the system in detail, you can check out our MacBook Air M5 review. We've also left a handful of our findings in the gallery above. Sporting excellent battery life, a comfortable keyboard, MagSafe charging, and Apple's Center Stage Camera, you'll also get a duo of Thunderbolt 4 ports around the side to plug in any docks to increase the amount of I/O.

Both 13 and 15-inch models are virtually identical aside from screen size and battery capacity, so you cannot go wrong with either choice. Both models are available on Amazon in an array of different colors for you to choose from. These are long-lasting systems that are built to weather the years, especially if you're only planning on using it for light computing tasks. It's a notable step up in quality from the cheaper MacBook Neo, and it shows. — Sayem Ahmed

If you found yourself with a PC connected to a television, then it's likely that you don't want to mess around with any messy cables, find a mouse surface, or generally add more clutter than is necessary around the place. Logitech's K400 Plus has been the de facto couch keyboard and mouse for a long time, and there's simply nothing quite like it out there at such an accessible price. The combo has been discounted to $23.74 on Amazon, so if you're thinking about giving yourself an easier time typing stuff into your Steam Machine or other living room PC, you should grab this.

The Logitech K400 Plus offers a keyboard and trackpad combo that makes it ideal for couch-based computers and media PCs, with a series of media keys, an understated design, and fully wireless operation thanks to its included USB-A dongle.

The design might be nearing a decade old, but the functionality on offer here is key: measuring fourteen inches across and just 5.5 inches wide, this isn't exactly a huge keyboard, making it easy to hide beneath media units. Perhaps the most important thing is the lack of garish RGB lights, which you'll find on alternatives from other brands. Also, you'll practically never have to charge it, as the Logitech K400 Plus is rated for a battery life of up to 18 months.

Framework is releasing a challenger to this keyboard, but you could buy almost five of these Logitech boards for the price of a single alternative from Framework. If saving cash is the name of the game, it's hard to go wrong here. — Sayem Ahmed

This Best Buy exclusive config of the Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 has just gotten a lovely discount for the Black Friday weekend. Packing in this much power into a compact chassis makes it the ideal portable premium gaming workstation. Another thing to note here is that you also get the full-powered version of the RTX 5070 Ti here, offering 12GB of VRAM at a 115W TGP, meaning you're not leaving any performance on the table.

The ROG Zephyrus G14 sports an Intel Core Ultra 386H with 16 cores and threads (4P and 8E cores), with a boost clock of up to 4.9 GHz. The system is complemented by the RTX 5070 Ti 12GB, 16GB of DDR5-8533, a 1TB NVMe SSD, and a 3K OLED display.

Because of the form factor on offer here, you won't get user-upgradable RAM, as the system's 16GB of LPDDR5X is soldered on. You can however, add another NVMe SSD, should you find things get a little tight with larger game installs. The highlight is the 2880 x 1800 OLED display, which can get plenty bright. Alongside all this is onboard Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4, a host of ports including Thunderbolt 4 support for any higher-end docks, and a six-speaker system.

As one of the more premium gaming laptops on the market, the Zephyrus G14 manages to strike a balance between performance and portability, which means that you'll not have to deadlift it to take it off your desk, unlike some of the gaming laptop behemoths that inhabit the high-end of the spectrum. With almost $600 off at Best Buy, get it while the deals are still hot. — Sayem Ahmed

AceMagic’s F5A mini PC sports AMD’s Gorgon Point Ryzen AI 9 HX 470 silicon, with 12 cores and 24 threads, and a boost clock of up to 5.2 GHz, alongside an integrated AMD Radeon 890M, 32GB of DDR5-5600 memory, and 1TB of NVMe storage. The PC has now been discounted by 27% on Amazon, which makes this one of the better mini PC deals that we’ve seen so far.

The AceMagic F5A Mini PC is powered by an AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 470 with Radeon 890M integrated graphics, sports 32GB of DDR5-5600 RAM, 1TB of NVMe storage, and offers WI-Fi 7 support out of the box, with an additional OcuLink port for further expandability.

The AceMagic F5A appears on paper to be a performant little machine, boasting several USB4 Ports, 2.5GB Ethernet, and coming in a small package, with room for storage expandability. After an unfortunate power-supply failure earlier this year, I had to switch to using a system with the same specs for over a week, and I was surprised at how much AMD’s modern APUs can handle in productivity-related tasks, and even light video editing.

This is the cheapest Gorgon Point-based Mini PC on Amazon right now, and if you’re after a small system with further support for eGPUs through an OcuLink port, the AceMagic F5A Mini should be on your radar. — Sayem Ahmed

You know that hard drive? Yeah, that one that's like a decade old that's been sitting in your drawer. It's probably going to fail at some point, and when it does, you don't want to be caught out without a handy backup of the data stored on there, lest you lose all of those precious files, photos and memories. With UGreen's dual-bay HDD drive cloner, you can safely back up that ancient drive onto something newer, perhaps a deal you find on a new drive this Black Friday.

The UGreen Dual-Bay HDD docking station supports two SATA HDDs at both 2.5 and 3.5 inch sizes. The device includes a wireless cloning feature and plugs into your PC from a Micro-B to USB-C/A cable.

Using the station, which supports both 2.5-inch and 3.5-inch drives, you can use the on-device offline cloning feature to copy all of your files without having to connect it up to a PC. Should you choose to plug it in, it also works as a desktop dock for any storage you'd like to hook up to a given system. UGreen touts up to 5Gbps speeds across the dock and its included cable. The device also requires a 12V power adaptor to function, so if you're looking to make this a permanent feature on your desk, be sure to ensure you have enough plug sockets around to make it work.

Otherwise, this is a handy device, especially for cloning older drives. It's not a given that a laptop has support for old SATA drives these days, so if you're looking to go diving through your archives of old HDDs or systems, this will no doubt save you a few headaches. — Sayem Ahmed

8BitDo's controllers are, broadly speaking, excellent. Its SN30 controller carries with it a clearly SNES-inspired look, with modern features like dual analog joysticks and compatibility across PC, Android, Mac, Windows, and Steam. The controller itself has been out for quite some time, but recently 8BitDo upgraded the SN30 to feature magnetic Hall Effect joysticks.

With its SNES-inspired design, this controller will entice gamers of a certain age. But its appeal goes beyond its looks, with Hall Effect joysticks and support for the Switch 1 and 2, PC, macOS, and basically any OS that supports games and Bluetooth.

Luckily, it's this upgraded Hall Effect-equipped version of the controller that's gone on sale. You get a suite of modern controls, like clickable L3 and R3 buttons, rumble, motion controls, and Bluetooth. Just note that given the size and layout of the SN30, the only thing it omits is analog triggers.

After receiving a firmware update, the pad can also be used on the Nintendo Switch 2 across any title that supports a Pro Controller. This gives it a wide range of versatility across platforms, but do be warned: the smaller size of the pad can take a while to get used to, and for those with larger hands, you might find this to be a little uncomfortable. But, at this price point, it's difficult to argue with the value on offer here. I own two of these controllers, but sadly the fancy transparent versions aren't on sale this time around. These pads are perfect for playing old retro platformers and beat-em-ups like Streets of Rage 4. — Sayem Ahmed

If you want chart-topping gaming and productivity performance in a single CPU, AMD's 16-core X3D chips are uncontested. They both provide gaming performance on par with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, top the charts in multithreaded productivity applications, and are in a close second place to Intel's Arrow Lake Refresh in single-threaded apps. Both CPUs are on deep discount for Black Friday, with the dual-CCD Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 hitting an all-time low at $759.

Okay, now AMD's chart-topping Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 might not be the CPU to choose if you're looking for overall value, but if you're after a multithreaded productivity workhorse that stands on par with Intel's best, while also offering the gaming performance of the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, it might be worth a look. Yesterday we spotted that the cache-abundant CPU hit an all-time-low price, with a $140 discount at Amazon, making its price a little bit more palatable. If you're not in need of AMD's biggest and best, then you can also grab a solid $115 discount on the 9950X3D.

The Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 is AMD's first dual-CCD CPU with 3D V-Cache. It sports 16 cores and 192 MB of L3 cache, and it can boost up to 5.6 GHz.

The Ryzen 9 9950X3D features 128MB of L3 cache, which enables it to claim the title of the fastest gaming chip on the market. It features 16 Zen 5 cores and 32 threads of computing power, reaching a peak clock speed of 5.7 GHz.

Both CPUs feature 16 Zen 5 cores and 32 threads, along with AMD's stacked 3D V-Cache. The main difference is that the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 has that stacked across on both of its two CCDs, while the Ryzen 9 9950X3D only has the stacked cache on a single CCD. To accommodate the extra cache, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 also has a 100 MHz reduction in maximum boost clock, topping out at 5.6 GHz compared to 5.7 GHz on the 9950X3D.

The pair of CPUs feature a total of 16 cores and 32 threads, based on AMD's Zen 5 architecture, and utilize a stacked 3D V-Cache, which gives both chips an edge in gaming. If you're looking at the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, the difference between the two is that the aforementioned cache is spread across both CCDs, instead of just the one on the 9950X3D. The 9950X3D2 also has slightly lower clock speeds, boosting to 5.6 GHz instead of the 5.7 GHz seen on the 9950X3D. To help you pick, we've dropped a bunch of performance charts below.

There's a 4% difference between the 9950X3D2 and 9900X3D in productivity workloads, and generally speaking, most people won't notice the difference between the two, as in gaming workloads, the chips are pretty much identical. If you want to save some cash, and some cache, choose the 9950X3D. If you want top-class performance at a top-shelf price, choose the 9950X3D2. — Sayem Ahmed

SanDisk’s 2TB Optimus GX Pro 8100 PCIe 5.0 SSD got a $95 discount and hit an all-time low of $349 over at Amazon. The drive itself boasts up to 14,900 MB/s read speeds and 14,000 MB/s write speeds, almost completely saturating the bandwidth available on its Silicon Motion SM2508 PCIe 5.0 x4 controller. The Optimus GX Pro 8100 uses Kioxia's BiCS8 218-layer TLC 3D CBA NAND, paired with 2GB of DDR4-3200 memory for use as a cache for fast, bursty work.

Expand your internal storage with SanDisk's 2TB Optimus GX Pro 8100 PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSD. This speedy drive offers 14,900/14,000 r/w speeds and has a 5-year warranty.

The overall price of the SanDisk Optimus GX Pro 8100 means that you'll be grabbing this incredibly fast storage at a mere 18 cents per gigabyte, which is stellar value for a PCIe 5.0 drive such as this, and it's one of the lowest prices we've seen a 2TB PCIe 5.0 drive drop to this Black Friday weekend.

When we benchmarked the 8TB version of this SSD, we found that under certain conditions, it managed to beat out Samsung's 9100 Pro. In addition to being super quick and cheaper than its closest rivals, you can also expect to get a five-year limited warranty in case things go awry. – Sayem Ahmed

Getting a good HDD deal in this market is a rare thing, and this deal we spotted yesterday over at Newegg for an external 16TB Seagate HDD works out to just two cents per gigabyte. Yes, it uses a USB 3.0 interface, but for cold storage of larger files, images, or video, you don't really need blisteringly fast transfer speeds in the first place. Coming in at $399.99, Seagate's External HDD might be the answer to all of your storage woes, or just offer you necessary extra room.

The Seagate Expansion Desktop drive is a 16TB HDD that connects via USB 3.0. It's formatted to ExFAT by default, allowing it to work with virtually any platform, straight out of the box. The device is powered by an included AC power cable, and connects to your system over a Micro-B to USB-A connector.

The Seagate 16TB drive inside is usually easily shuckable, though do take care in doing so if that's your intention: Usually we'll see a white-labelled drive, and it's easy to accidentally damage the HDD while doing so. However, if you're brave enough to void your warranty, it could be a worthwhile endeavor. Getting a 16TB HDD anywhere else will cost much more, so if you're up for a bit of risk-reward, it could make for a solid extra internal drive, or suitable for use in a NAS.

The Micro-B to USB-A connector is a touch outdated in 2026, but if it's still going to be fast enough for transferring files. If you shuck the drive itself, expect standard SATA power and data connectors instead. It's difficult to argue with the price-per-gigabyte on this deal, so if you're looking to upgrade your storage this holiday, don't sleep on this Newegg deal. — Sayem Ahmed

Intel's Core Ultra 270K plus lives on our list of the best CPUs for gaming for a good reason; not only is it adept at crunching through the latest games, but it's also our top pick for anyone looking for a top-shelf productivity workhorse. Intel's latest and greatest CPU is listed at $269 at Newegg, but it also comes with a stackable code, knocking the price down to $249 with a handful of free gifts: A Rosewill 360mm AIO liquid cooler, in addition to an Intel Gaming Bundle where you can pick from two free titles, including Total War: Warhammer 40,000, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and more.

Get Intel's latest and greatest processor, the 270K Plus. The 8p/16e core processor has plenty of oomph to plow through any workflow and games well, too.

The Intel Core Ultra 270K Plus manages to go toe-to-toe in gaming performance with AMD's Ryzen 7 7800X3D, and is one of the best CPUs available now in productivity workloads. Sporting a total of 24 cores, split into 8 P-Cores and 16 E-Cores, the configuration actually matches the same core config as the much pricier Core Ultra 9 285K. Boasting clock speeds of up to 5.5GHz, this is a seasonal offer you don't want to miss out on. — Sayem Ahmed

Following its short-lived Galaxy Z TriFold, Samsung appears to have a sequel on the way that’s set to arrive in the Galaxy Z Fold 9 lineup.

The Galaxy Z TriFold launched a few months after the Galaxy Z Fold 7, carrying the codename “Q7m.” GalaxyClub now reports that “Q9m” has surfaced, implying that Galaxy Z TriFold 2 will be based on the Galaxy Z Fold 9 series.

For one, don’t expect a new TriFold to arrive in the same schedule as the first one. The original Galaxy Z TriFold launched in late 2025 before expanding to other regions in early 2026. While it’s abundantly clear we’re not getting a new model before the year lets out, this codename effectively rules out a release before the Galaxy Z Fold 9 series launches which, assuming it follows the usual schedule, won’t happen until around July.

This also tells us that the Galaxy Z TriFold 2 will be based on the Galaxy Z Fold 9 series, likely including the latest chipset and Samsung’s Android 18 build.

There’s no guarantee yet about when the next TriFold might debut, how much it might cost, or where it might launch. GalaxyClub notes that the codename subtly suggests there’s no EU release in the plans, but it can’t be completely ruled out either.

Whatever happens with Galaxy Z TriFold 2, let’s just hope it lasts longer than the original.

#10281. GTA VI developers vote against unionization

Workers voted 75 percent against the IWGB recognition agreement.

Workers voted 75 percent against the IWGB recognition agreement.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Workers at Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games won’t unionize, after the vote for a formal recognition agreement failed, with only 25 percent of votes in favor of unionization. The Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) said that Rockstar workers in the union will continue organizing even without formal recognition.

Voting ran from November 12th through 26th, covering the launch of GTA VI. If successful, the vote would have established a formal framework for collective negotiation with the studio over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, and pensions, along with a right to consultation over future changes including AI implementation and layoffs. Without it, Rockstar won’t have an obligation to meet union representatives, though workers and union members can still lobby for change informally.

“For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society - this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for,” IWGB said in a statement sent to The Verge. “Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.”

When Rockstar fired 31 IWGB members last year, the union accused it of “the most blatant and ruthless act of union busting in the history of the games industry.” That case has gone to a UK employment tribunal, with a judgment still pending.

“We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI,” Rockstar head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe told Bloomberg News. “This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”

#10278. Your AI Pipeline Works. But Can You Trust It?

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI is becoming a part of almost everything we do in technology today. Whether it's detecting fraudulent transactions, assessing credit risk, forecasting demand, or personalizing customer experiences, organizations are increasingly relying on AI to make faster and smarter decisions.

And naturally, when we talk about building AI systems, most of the conversation revolves around model accuracy, performance, and deployment. We spend considerable time making sure our models are trained well, our pipelines run efficiently, and our systems can handle production workloads.

But here's something we don't always pay enough attention to: Can we actually trust the data feeding these models?

After all, even the most sophisticated AI model can produce misleading results if the underlying data is incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrectly interpreted. What's interesting is that these problems don't always show up as technical failures. Sometimes, everything appears to be working perfectly fine.

Imagine a financial institution that has recently deployed an AI-powered loan risk assessment system. The team has spent months preparing the data, training the model, testing its performance, and finally moving it into production.

The deployment goes smoothly. Data pipelines are running on schedule, predictions are being generated, and all the monitoring dashboards are green.

A few weeks later, however, the business team notices something unusual. The model has started classifying more customers as high risk than expected.

The data science team checks the model configuration. Nothing has changed. The engineering team reviews the pipelines. All jobs have completed successfully. Even the infrastructure looks healthy.

It turns out that an upstream source system changed the definition of a customer income field from annual gross income to annual net income. The field name remained the same, the data type was still numeric, and none of the existing technical validations detected the change.

The pipeline continued running as expected, but the model was now receiving information with a different business meaning.

This brings us to an important point: Just because an AI pipeline runs successfully doesn't necessarily mean we can trust its output.

Building reliable AI systems requires us to look beyond the model itself. We need to understand where the data originates, how it changes as it moves through different systems, whether it meets quality expectations, and who is responsible when something goes wrong.

In this article, we'll explore three important elements of trustworthy AI pipelines (data quality, data lineage, and accountability) and look at how engineering teams can incorporate them into their existing workflows without making the process unnecessarily complicated.

Most modern data pipelines come with some form of operational monitoring. Engineering teams track job completion, execution time, system availability, and processing failures.

These metrics are important because they help us understand whether our systems are functioning as expected.

Operational monitoring primarily tells us whether a pipeline executed successfully. It doesn't necessarily tell us whether the data being processed is accurate, consistent, or suitable for the model consuming it.

Suppose we're building a loan risk model that uses a customer's debt-to-income ratio as one of its input features.

Debt-to-income ratio = Monthly debt payments / Monthly income

Now imagine that an upstream system starts supplying annual income instead of monthly income.

The calculation still executes successfully. The values are numeric, the transformation doesn't throw an error, and the model continues generating predictions.

However, the resulting debt-to-income ratio is incorrect because the numerator and denominator represent different time periods.

This is where traditional monitoring falls short.

To build trustworthy AI pipelines, we need to look at different dimensions of system health.

A pipeline can be operationally healthy while processing unreliable data. Similarly, a model can continue producing predictions even when the meaning of an important input field has changed.

For engineering teams, the objective should be to identify these problems as early as possible, ideally before they reach downstream models.

We've all heard the phrase "garbage in, garbage out."

And despite all the progress we've made in artificial intelligence, this principle hasn't changed.

AI models may be capable of processing enormous volumes of data and identifying complex patterns, but they cannot automatically guarantee that the information they're receiving is correct.

This is where data quality becomes important.

Data quality refers to how well information meets the requirements of its intended use. In AI pipelines, it helps us determine whether incoming data is sufficiently reliable for model training, evaluation, or inference.

Let's look at four dimensions that are particularly relevant.

Imagine we're developing a loan risk model that relies on customer income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

What happens if 20% of the incoming records are missing income information?

Should we reject those records? Should we replace missing values using an approved statistical method? Or should we flag them for additional review?

There isn't one answer that works for every system.

The right approach depends on the model, the business requirements, and the potential consequences of the decision.

What matters is that missing information is handled deliberately.

For example, replacing missing income with zero may allow the pipeline to continue running, but it could significantly distort the model's predictions.

Validity checks whether values meet expected formats, ranges, and business rules.

Consider a customer record containing the following information:

The credit utilization value immediately stands out.

Although credit utilization can exceed 100% in certain circumstances, a value of 450% may warrant investigation.

This highlights an important distinction: Not every unusual value is incorrect, and not every technically valid value is meaningful.

A database may accept any numeric value, but the business may need additional rules to determine whether that value is appropriate for the model.

Engineering teams should distinguish between invalid records, unexpected observations, and legitimate exceptions.

This is one of the most common challenges in enterprise data environments.

Imagine two systems providing customer income information.

Both datasets contain a column called income.

If we combine these datasets without understanding their definitions, we risk introducing inconsistencies into downstream calculations.

The data may look perfectly fine from a technical perspective. The problem is that the same field represents different business concepts.

This is why data definitions, units, and transformation rules are just as important as schema validation.

Suppose a model predicts a customer's current financial risk using income information that was last updated 18 months ago.

The data might be accurate, complete, and consistent.

But is it current enough to support the decision?

Different AI applications have different freshness requirements.

A real-time fraud detection model may require near-real-time transaction information, while a long-term forecasting model may work with less frequently updated datasets.

The important thing is to define these expectations based on how the data will be used.

The good news is that improving data quality doesn't always require sophisticated enterprise tools.

A practical starting point is to define validation rules for the most important input fields.

For example, consider the following conceptual configuration:

This is an illustrative data quality contract rather than executable configuration for a particular framework.

It defines basic expectations and specifies what should happen when the data fails validation.

Tools such as Great Expectations can help automate these checks. For smaller systems, custom SQL or Python validations may be sufficient.

However, technical validation alone isn't enough.

Remember our original example where the income field changed from gross to net income?

Both values could easily pass a rule requiring income to be greater than zero.

Detecting that kind of issue requires clear business definitions, communication with upstream systems, and appropriate change management.

In other words, data quality isn't just about checking values. It's also about understanding what those values represent.

Now let's assume our loan risk model generates an unexpectedly high risk score for a customer.

The model output is available, but we want to understand what contributed to the prediction.

The income information came from a customer application system. Outstanding debt came from another database. Both datasets went through several transformations before reaching the feature engineering pipeline.

The final features were then passed to the model.

At this point, a seemingly simple question becomes surprisingly difficult:

Where exactly did the information used for this prediction come from?

This is where data lineage becomes valuable.

Data lineage describes how data originates, moves, and changes across different systems.

For AI pipelines, it helps us understand the journey from raw source data to the features used by a model.

Source Systems → Data Transformation → Feature Engineering → Model Inference → Predictions

Each stage introduces dependencies that can affect downstream results.

Data lineage can be captured at different levels of detail.

Dataset-level lineage shows relationships between datasets.

Loan Applications → Cleaned Applications → Model Features

This helps us understand how datasets move through the overall architecture.

However, suppose the model's debt-to-income ratio suddenly changes.

Dataset-level lineage might tell us which datasets were involved, but it may not provide enough detail to identify the affected field.

That's where column-level lineage becomes useful.

debt_to_income_ratio = monthly_debt_payment / monthly_income

Column-level lineage can show that the resulting feature depends on two upstream attributes.

If one of those attributes changes, engineers can trace the dependency and investigate the impact.

This is especially valuable in environments where multiple reports, applications, and AI models depend on shared data sources.

Large organizations may use dedicated metadata management and lineage platforms.

However, smaller teams can start by capturing essential metadata during pipeline execution.

OpenLineage provides an open standard for collecting and exchanging lineage metadata across supported systems.

It's important to understand that lineage doesn't automatically guarantee data accuracy.

A pipeline can be perfectly documented and still contain incorrect transformation logic.

But when something goes wrong, lineage gives engineering teams a clearer starting point for investigation.

Instead of searching across multiple systems and trying to reconstruct dependencies manually, they can identify where data originated and how it changed along the way.

An AI model starts producing unexpected results.

The data science team checks the model and finds no issues.

The data engineering team confirms that the pipelines are running successfully.

The source-system team verifies that data was delivered according to its interface.

Everyone has completed their individual checks, but nobody has identified who should coordinate the investigation.

This is where accountability becomes important.

AI pipelines often involve multiple teams responsible for different stages of the data lifecycle. Without clearly defined ownership, even relatively simple issues can take longer to resolve.

A practical accountability framework should distinguish between three responsibilities.

Data owners are responsible for defining the business meaning and expected quality of critical information.

For example, someone needs to determine whether an income field represents gross income, net income, or another financial measure.

These definitions should be documented and communicated to downstream consumers.

Data engineering and platform teams typically manage data ingestion, transformations, validation mechanisms, and pipeline operations.

Their responsibilities may include implementing quality checks, monitoring failures, and assessing the technical impact of changes.

However, technical teams shouldn't be expected to make business-definition decisions without appropriate input.

Data science and ML engineering teams are responsible for evaluating model behavior, managing model versions, and assessing how changes in input data may affect predictions.

If a critical feature changes, the model team may need to determine whether additional testing, recalibration, or retraining is required.

Defining ownership is useful, but connecting it to an operational process is even more important.

Consider a critical data quality failure during feature generation.

The exact workflow will vary depending on the organization and the risk associated with the application.

The objective is to ensure that technical alerts lead to clear actions.

After all, an alert that nobody owns is just another notification waiting to be ignored.

So far, we've discussed why data quality, lineage, and accountability matter.

But how can we bring these concepts into everyday engineering practices?

Here are five controls that teams can introduce without redesigning their entire architecture.

Data contracts define expectations between data producers and consumers.

They can document schemas, field definitions, units, freshness requirements, and compatibility expectations.

For example, rather than specifying only that annual_income is numeric, a contract should clarify whether it represents gross or net income, the currency, and the applicable time period.

This reduces the risk of downstream systems misinterpreting technically valid information.

Quality gates validate critical data before it progresses through the pipeline.

These checks can be implemented during ingestion, transformation, feature generation, or inference.

For example, a feature engineering process calculating debt-to-income ratios should verify that debt and income values use compatible time periods.

Failure handling should reflect the severity of the issue. Some records may be quarantined, while more serious failures may require stopping the pipeline.

Pipeline execution should produce sufficient metadata to identify source datasets, transformations, and downstream outputs.

Where appropriate, teams should also capture model and feature versions associated with predictions.

This information supports impact analysis, debugging, and investigation when unexpected results occur.

Datasets change, transformation logic is updated, features are modified, and models are retrained.

Versioning helps engineering teams understand which components were active at a particular point in time.

Relevant evidence may include pipeline configurations, dataset snapshots, model versions, validation outcomes, and deployment records.

Every critical data element or pipeline component should have an identified owner or responsible team.

More importantly, ownership should connect directly to incident management and change approval processes.

If a source definition changes, teams should know who evaluates the impact.

If a quality gate fails, the responsible team should receive the alert.

If model performance deteriorates, the investigation should have a clear escalation path.

These controls are most effective when they become part of normal development and deployment practices rather than separate administrative activities.

Implementing comprehensive governance across an entire data environment can be challenging, particularly for organizations with legacy systems and complex dependencies.

A more effective approach is to begin with one critical AI pipeline.

For example, a team operating a loan risk model could start by identifying the inputs that have the greatest influence on its predictions.

These might include income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

For each critical input, the team can document five things:

Once these foundations are established, the team can implement automated checks and gradually extend the approach to additional datasets.

This incremental strategy also makes it easier to demonstrate the value of governance controls.

For instance, teams can track how quickly data-related incidents are detected, how long investigations take, and whether recurring issues are reduced.

The goal isn't to introduce governance for its own sake.

It's to improve the reliability, maintainability, and transparency of the systems developers are responsible for operating.

Explainable AI has become an important topic in machine learning.

Techniques such as feature importance analysis and SHAP can help teams understand which inputs influence model predictions.

However, explainability and data trustworthiness address different problems.

Suppose a model explanation identifies debt-to-income ratio as a major contributor to a customer's high-risk classification.

That explanation may accurately describe the model's behavior.

But if the debt-to-income ratio was calculated using an incorrectly defined income field, the explanation alone may not reveal the underlying data issue.

This highlights the importance of evaluating AI systems across multiple dimensions.

Model explainability helps us understand how predictions are generated.

Data quality helps establish whether inputs satisfy defined expectations.

Data lineage provides visibility into where information originated and how it was transformed.

Accountability ensures that identified problems can be investigated and addressed.

These capabilities are complementary rather than interchangeable.

None independently guarantees that an AI system is accurate, fair, secure, or compliant. Together, however, they provide a stronger foundation for evaluating and improving system reliability.

As AI systems become more integrated into business processes, engineering teams face increasing expectations around reliability, transparency, and accountability.

Model accuracy and operational performance remain essential, but they represent only part of the overall picture.

A pipeline can execute successfully while processing inconsistent information. A model can generate predictions using features whose definitions have changed. And an explanation can describe a model's behavior without identifying problems in the underlying data.

Building trustworthy AI therefore requires attention to the entire data lifecycle.

Data quality controls help detect unreliable inputs. Lineage provides visibility into how information moves through systems. Clear ownership ensures that issues can be investigated and resolved.

Importantly, these practices don't need to begin with large-scale governance programs or expensive technology investments.

Engineering teams can start with a single critical pipeline, identify its most important data elements, establish quality expectations, and introduce basic traceability and accountability mechanisms.

Over time, these practices can become part of standard development and deployment workflows.

The real measure of a trustworthy AI pipeline isn't simply whether it produces a prediction. It's whether the organization can understand, validate, and take responsibility for the information behind that prediction.

After all, a green dashboard is reassuring. But it shouldn't be the only evidence that an AI system is working as intended.

#10276. Grand Theft Auto VI is a different kind of GTA — so it needed a different kind of ending

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.

GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In most Grand Theft Auto games, and most open-world games for that matter, the world is left open for you to explore once the credits roll. It could be Los Santos or a twisted take on Manhattan, but the idea is that the main story is just one part of the experience. After that’s done, there are usually still places you haven’t explored or side missions you left lingering. But Grand Theft Auto VI doesn’t work quite the same way. Because of its storyline, which involves a couple trying to get out of the criminal life for good, that kind of ending didn’t really fit.

“In this one it didn’t make sense,” Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North, told me ahead of the game’s launch. “Their story needed to end and have some kind of conclusion.”

This story contains light spoilers for the ending of Grand Theft Auto VI, along with a key plot point from chapter 1.

To be clear, you can still play GTA VI after the main storyline wraps up. But in order for that to happen, you have to zip back in time to a moment before a pivotal decision — I won’t spoil it for you — that alters the lives of main characters Jason and Lucia, along with their young son Tomás, who they’re attempting to get custody of. Nelson says the team tried “all sorts of things” but soon realized that “in no way did it make sense” to have the game end like a traditional GTA experience.

“Their story needed to end and have some kind of conclusion.”

“You go back and have this open time again where you have the best single-player safehouse you’ve ever had in a GTA, with a garage full of supercars, a helipad, a gym, and all of the stuff you could ever want,” he says of the solution the studio landed on. “And you can spend as long as you want there. But you don’t have Tommy. So the characters don’t have the one thing that they wanted at the start. There’s the tension where you have to spend some extra time grinding to make some more money without knowing what it’s going to get you, and it plays out differently if you get that money.”

One advantage of this structure is that it lets you try out different endings. GTA VI’s story can wrap up in multiple ways based on a variety of factors: how much money you have saved up, what kind of criminal you were throughout the game, and some key decisions you’re forced to make in the final moments. The new postgame structure creates an opportunity to see some of the alternate ways the story can go. “There’s a large number of potential outcomes based on how you played it,” Nelson says.

And at least in raster titles, the power of the RTX 5060 Ti plus the performance boost offered by DLSS 4.5 upscaling means you might even be able to explore 1440p gaming, too. Get this power-packed system for less as we roll into the Black Friday weekend. -- Jeff Kampman

#10270. How Developers Can Detect Fake Payment Gateways and Build Secure Checkout Integrations

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Online payments are an essential part of modern web applications. E-commerce platforms, subscription services, and online marketplaces all depend on payment gateways to process transactions and manage customer orders.

However, integrating a payment gateway involves more than adding a payment button or displaying a checkout form. Developers must ensure that payment requests are sent to legitimate providers, transaction information is validated correctly, and payment confirmations cannot be manipulated.

Fake payment gateways introduce another challenge. They can imitate legitimate payment interfaces, use copied checkout templates, and redirect customers to fraudulent websites. Even when a checkout page looks professional, its underlying implementation may not be trustworthy.

For developers, understanding these risks is important when designing payment workflows. This article explores common payment integration vulnerabilities and practical techniques for building secure checkout systems using JavaScript and Node.js.

A payment gateway connects an application with a payment processing service. It handles transaction requests and communicates payment results to the merchant's application.

A typical checkout process involves several components:

A frontend checkout interface where customers review their orders.

A backend application that creates payment requests.

A payment provider that processes transactions.

A webhook endpoint that receives payment notifications.

A database that stores order and transaction information.

Attackers can target different parts of this process.

For example, a fraudulent website may copy the appearance of a legitimate checkout page while sending submitted information to an unauthorized server. Another approach involves manipulating payment requests or creating fake confirmation pages that make an unsuccessful transaction appear complete.

These techniques are also relevant to marketplace fraud. An eBay scam can involve fraudulent payment requests and misleading transaction links, illustrating why developers need to consider payment security beyond the appearance of a checkout page.

The important distinction is that a legitimate-looking interface does not establish that the payment request is reaching an authorized provider.

One of the first steps in reviewing a payment integration is checking where the application sends its payment requests.

Developers should inspect network requests using browser developer tools. The Network tab can reveal which domains receive requests when a customer opens the checkout page or submits a payment form.

Look for unexpected requests, unfamiliar domains, and scripts loaded from sources that are not part of the approved integration.

For example, a checkout application might load a payment script like this:

The URL above is illustrative, not an actual payment provider.

Developers should compare the script URL and integration method with the provider's official documentation rather than trusting a URL simply because it appears familiar.

Reviewing external JavaScript dependencies.

Checking whether payment forms submit data to approved endpoints.

Confirming that HTTPS is used throughout the payment process.

Reviewing changes to payment-related scripts during development.

A Content Security Policy (CSP) can also restrict which domains are allowed to load scripts and receive certain types of requests.

These example domains must be replaced with the actual domains documented by the selected payment provider.

A carefully configured policy can reduce the risk of unauthorized scripts and unexpected form submissions.

A common mistake in payment development is trusting values submitted directly from the browser.

Consider an application where the frontend sends an order ID and payment amount to the backend.

An attacker could modify the amount before submitting the request. If the backend accepts that value without checking the original order, the application may create a payment session for an incorrect amount.

The safer approach is to retrieve the order from the database and calculate the amount on the server.

Here, payment Gateway create Checkout Session() represents a provider-specific server-side SDK method.

The important part is that the backend retrieves the amount from its own database rather than accepting a price supplied by the customer.

Developers should also validate product IDs, quantities, discounts, currency, and order ownership before creating a payment session.

This prevents frontend manipulation from directly determining the final transaction amount.

Developers should avoid building payment processing around unverified scripts, copied templates, or unknown third-party services.

Instead, use official APIs and SDKs provided by established payment processors.

A hosted checkout integration is one common option. The merchant's backend creates a payment session through the provider's API, and the customer is redirected to the provider's hosted checkout page.

This approach can reduce the amount of sensitive card information handled by the merchant's application.

However, developers still need to configure the integration correctly.

Store secret API keys in server-side environment variables or a secrets manager.

Never expose private credentials in frontend JavaScript.

Use the provider's official SDK where available.

Validate checkout session creation on the backend.

Restrict success and cancellation URLs to approved destinations.

Use HTTPS for application and payment communication.

Developers should also understand the difference between public and secret API credentials. Public keys may be designed for browser use, while secret keys must remain on the server.

The OWASP Third-Party Payment Gateway Integration Cheat Sheet provides additional guidance on securing payment requests, validating transaction details, and handling payment callbacks.

Payment providers often use webhooks to notify applications when transactions are completed, failed, or refunded.

However, webhook endpoints are publicly accessible URLs in many integrations. Without proper verification, an attacker may send a fabricated HTTP request that looks like a successful payment notification.

Developers should verify webhook signatures using the payment provider's official SDK.

Consider this simplified Node.js example:

The verify Webhook() method represents the signature verification functionality of a payment provider's SDK. It is not a universal Node.js method.

The example also assumes that the provider's event contains the relevant order and transaction details. Developers should follow the provider's actual event schema and retrieve the authoritative payment status when required.

The application should never mark an order as paid simply because a customer has reached a success URL.

Instead, payment confirmation should depend on an authenticated provider notification or a server-side verification request.

Another important issue in payment development is duplicate processing.

Imagine a customer clicks the payment button twice because the first request takes too long. The application may create two payment sessions or attempt to charge the customer more than once.

Network interruptions and automatic retries can create similar situations.

Idempotency helps prevent these problems by ensuring that repeated requests with the same idempotency key do not create duplicate operations.

A simplified example using Node.js might look like this:

The example uses a provider-specific idempotency option. Actual SDK syntax and key requirements vary between providers.

In a production application, developers should also store payment attempts in the database and enforce appropriate uniqueness constraints.

This helps maintain consistent transaction records even when requests are repeated or interrupted.

A payment integration should be tested beyond the normal successful checkout process.

Most established payment providers offer sandbox environments that allow developers to simulate transactions without charging real customers.

These environments are useful for testing different transaction scenarios.

Developers should also test whether the application handles provider downtime correctly.

For example, if the payment provider becomes temporarily unavailable, the application should not mark an order as completed or assume that the transaction succeeded.

Automated integration tests can help verify these scenarios before deployment. Monitoring payment failures, unexpected status changes, and repeated webhook errors can also help developers identify problems after release.

Security does not end when a payment integration goes live.

Developers should implement monitoring to identify unusual transaction patterns and unexpected changes in payment behavior.

Recording payment attempts and transaction IDs.

Monitoring webhook signature verification failures.

Detecting repeated requests for the same order.

Alerting on unexpected order status changes.

However, logging must be implemented carefully.

Applications should never store card verification codes or expose secret API keys in application logs. Sensitive information should be excluded from debugging output, and access to transaction records should be restricted.

Developers should also follow the payment provider's security requirements and applicable PCI DSS obligations when handling payment data.

Detecting fake payment gateways and building secure checkout integrations requires more than checking whether a payment page looks legitimate.

Developers need to examine the complete transaction flow, validate payment information on the server, use official payment APIs, verify webhook signatures, and prevent duplicate transactions.

JavaScript and Node.js provide useful tools for implementing these security controls, but the reliability of a payment system ultimately depends on how its frontend, backend, database, and payment provider communicate.

A well-designed checkout integration should verify every important transaction before fulfilling an order. By following these development practices, teams can build payment systems that are easier to maintain, more reliable, and better protected against common payment manipulation techniques.

#10267. This gaming mouse should be a Logitech-killer, but it has one big flaw

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Keychron’s G6 HE uses magnetic switches like Logitech’s Superstrike mice, but the clicks are all off.﻿

Keychron’s G6 HE uses magnetic switches like Logitech’s Superstrike mice, but the clicks are all off.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When Keychron announced its $90 G6 HE gaming mouse, I immediately thought, “Cool! A cheaper alternative to the pricey $180 Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike.” Logitech’s innovation with the Superstrike is using magnetic Hall effect switches for a user-adjustable mouse click depth, with haptic vibrations mimicking the tactile click feel. The Keychron G6 HE, as its name indicates, also uses Hall effect switches for that same kind of customization. But something felt immediately off as I began testing it.

The mouse’s shape and design are very reminiscent of Logitech G Pro models, with more colorful flair. The magnetic switches are there and easily customizable (through a browser-based app, no less). But the clicks? The clicks are all wrong.

The left and right mouse buttons on the G6 HE use Keychron’s MagOptic switches, which are both magnetic Hall effect and optical. They click just like any standard mouse, regardless of where you set the actuation point. There are no fancy haptics on the Keychron. If you set the buttons to a shallow hair-trigger depth, you’ll register a press before you actually feel or hear any click. Set the depth for a very heavy press, and the mouse clicks before it actually registers. That… kind of defeats the purpose here.

There’s not much point in tuning the actuation depth of the G6 HE’s buttons if the click feel doesn’t match it. I suppose it’s still nice to have a hair-trigger-like setting for taking faster single shots in an FPS, but not feeling anything when you shoot is weird. And it gets frustrating when using the G6 HE as a regular mouse for productivity — like you’re getting phantom clicks as you mouse around your computer. At least I can feel my accidental clicks when using a Logitech Superstrike with the action set too high, and I know I’m to blame for leaving the mouse on my try-hard settings.

I reached out to Keychron for the reasoning behind the G6 HE’s magnetic-but-not-haptic setup, and cofounder Fab Chan said, “There are two reasons for this design. First, many users still prefer the feel of a traditional click over haptics. Second, a haptic motor adds weight, and for this model we prioritized a lighter design. That said, we’re planning a model with haptic feedback. It will be slightly heavier than the G6 HE, and we’ll share more details soon.”

The G6 HE is a lightweight mouse. It’s only 49g with its battery, or 40g in wired mode with the battery removed. The Logitech X2 Superstrike is 60g, and the newer X3 Superstrike is 59g — each still pretty light. If you ignore all the Hall effect stuff and just use the G6 HE as a regular mouse, it has some things going for it over the Superstrikes. In addition to its lighter build and much lower price, it feels a tiny bit comfier in my hand, thanks to its side walls that curve slightly inward at the bottom.

One of its best features is hot-swappable batteries. From my time testing Angry Miao’s AM Infinity Mouse, I know that once you can pop out a magnetic battery pack and quickly swap it, you never want to go back to plugging in your mouse to charge. You can also get the G6 HE in black with a standard built-in rechargeable battery for $15 less, but I don’t think that’s enough savings to forgo the convenience of hot-swap batteries.

The G6 HE’s charging base doubles as the wireless receiver, and of course it’s lit up with customizable RGB lighting. It has four programmable buttons for on-the-fly changes to things like DPI, lighting, mouse profiles, or just about anything else you want to program. The browser-based Keychron Launcher software is robust and makes tinkering with the G6 HE or its base very easy. And for some reason, the receiver / charging base is designed like a vacuum tube, which is fun, but it means you’re unscrewing its clear housing to access the battery — a little tedious.

I can’t shake my disappointment with the G6 HE’s lackadaisical magnetic switch implementation. Keychron seems proud of the fancy MagOptic Switch it put into the G6 HE, even going so far as to call it “next gen,” but this mouse seems a jack of all trades and master of none. The G6 HE is cheaper than most other mice with hot-swap batteries — which can still make it worthwhile if you don’t care about all the Hall effect stuff — but that is its lone saving grace.

We’ll have to wait and see if Keychron’s follow-up model with haptics can properly compete with the Superstrike mice and their hallmark feature. I’m excited to see where Hall effect tech goes in mice, and how more companies can evolve it, but the G6 HE is a half-measure.

Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge
